summary: Updates the Java bindings for GSS-API version 2, which give Java programmers uniform access to security services over different underlying mechanisms. It was replaced by RFC 8353.

plainLanguage.summary: Programs in Java need the right plugs to use GSS-API. This updates those plugs.

subtitle: Java language bindings for GSS-API security services

tldr.problem: Java applications need uniform access to security services like authentication, encryption, and delegation, but different cryptographic mechanisms (Kerberos, public-key systems) have different APIs. Java programmers need a common interface.
tldr.mechanism: GSS-API Java Bindings provide object-oriented interfaces and classes (GSSManager, GSSContext, GSSCredential, GSSName) that let applications authenticate principals, establish secure contexts, delegate rights, and apply per-message protection services, with pluggable support for multiple underlying mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: Java developers can write portable security-aware applications that work with any GSS-API mechanism. RFC 5653 updates RFC 2853 with clarifications based on implementation experience and now serves as the standard binding.

facts.label: Lifecycle methods
facts.value: acquire credentials, initSecContext()/acceptSecContext(), per-message ops, dispose()

today: RFC 5653 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2009 and obsoletes RFC 2853. It remains the normative specification for GSS-API Java bindings and has been widely implemented in Java security frameworks including the Java SE platform and enterprise application servers. It was itself replaced by RFC 8353 with further updates and clarifications.

sections.title: Overview of GSS-API and Security Services
sections.content:
The Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface (GSS-API) is a language-independent framework that lets application programmers access security services uniformly, regardless of the underlying cryptographic mechanism. GSS-API is defined conceptually in RFC 2743.

GSS-API provides three main capabilities: (1) authentication—a principal can prove its identity to another principal; (2) delegation—a principal can grant rights to another principal to act as an agent; and (3) per-message services—integrity checking and confidentiality (encryption) of individual application messages. These services work on top of various mechanisms like Kerberos 5 (RFC 4121) or Simple Public-Key GSS-API Mechanism (RFC 2025).

RFC 5653 specifies Java language bindings for GSS-API. The design aims to be object-oriented, support both system-wide and per-application installations of mechanisms, and leverage the Java Cryptography Architecture provider model for pluggable mechanism implementations. The bindings reside in the org.ietf.jgss package.
sections.plainLanguage: GSS-API is like a universal security plug that works with many different locks. Instead of learning how to use a Kerberos lock, an RSA lock, and a Diffie-Hellman lock separately, Java programmers can just use the GSS-API interface and swap mechanisms as needed.

sections.title: Four Stages of Using GSS-API
sections.content:
Applications using GSS-API follow four stages:

1) Acquire Credentials: The application obtains a credential object (GSSCredential) that proves its identity to other processes. A credential may contain multiple mechanism-specific credential elements, one per supported mechanism.

2) Establish Context: A pair of applications—an initiator and an acceptor—use their credentials to establish a security context (GSSContext). The initiator calls initSecContext() repeatedly, generating tokens that the acceptor processes with acceptSecContext(), until the context is established. During establishment, the initiator proves its identity to the acceptor. Optionally, the initiator can request mutual authentication (acceptor proves identity), credential delegation (acceptor receives delegated credentials to act as the initiator), or other services like replay detection.

3) Apply Per-Message Services: Once the context is established, both peers can protect application messages. The wrap() method applies confidentiality and integrity protection; the getMIC() method applies integrity and origin authentication only. Recipients call unwrap() or verifyMIC() to verify and extract the original message.

4) Clean Up: When communication ends, the application calls dispose() on the context to release cryptographic resources and invalidate the context.
sections.plainLanguage: First, get your credentials (your ID card). Second, shake hands with the other program by exchanging tokens until you trust each other. Third, use that trusted connection to send encrypted or signed messages. Fourth, clean up and go home.

sections.title: Core Classes and Interfaces
sections.content:
GSSManager is an abstract factory class (obtained via getInstance()) that creates GSS-API objects. It provides methods to list available mechanisms (getMechs()), query name types supported by mechanisms, and create names and credentials.

GSSName represents a principal identity. Applications create names from strings (e.g., 'user@example.com') or byte arrays using GSSManager.createName(). Names can be compared with equals(), converted to mechanism-specific names with canonicalize(), and exported to a portable byte array format.

GSSCredential encapsulates authentication data for one or more mechanisms. Applications acquire credentials for themselves (default principal) or for a specific identity, specifying the mechanism and intended usage (initiate, accept, or both). Credentials have lifetime and can be compared.

GSSContext represents one end of a security context. Initiators create it via GSSManager.createContext(); acceptors create it via GSSManager.createContext(myCred). Before calling initSecContext(), the initiator can request optional services like mutual authentication or confidentiality. After establishment, both peers use wrap()/unwrap() and getMIC()/verifyMIC() for per-message protection. Query methods reveal which services were actually negotiated.

MessageProp is a helper class for per-message operations. Applications pass it to wrap(), unwrap(), getMIC(), and verifyMIC() to set privacy preference and QOP (quality-of-protection), and to learn supplementary status (duplicate token, out-of-sequence token, etc.).

GSSException signals fatal errors using major and minor error codes, replacing C-style status code returns. Applications catch it to handle authentication failures, context errors, or mechanism-specific problems.

Oid represents Universal Object Identifiers used to identify mechanisms, name formats, and algorithm parameters. Oid objects are immutable and can be created from dotted notation (e.g., '1.2.840.113554.1.2.2' for Kerberos).

ChannelBinding specifies tags to bind a context to a particular communications channel, preventing context hijacking in multi-hop scenarios. Applications set channel bindings before context establishment.
sections.plainLanguage: GSSManager creates objects. GSSName is a principal identity. GSSCredential is your ID card. GSSContext is the secure connection. MessageProp tells wrap/unwrap whether to encrypt. Oid is a code for mechanisms. GSSException is an error. ChannelBinding locks the context to a specific channel.

sections.title: Optional Context Services and State
sections.content:
Context initiators can request optional services before calling initSecContext():

Mutual Authentication: Requests that the acceptor authenticate itself to the initiator. The initiator can query the result via getMutualAuthState(). Some mechanisms enable this automatically when other services are requested.

Delegation: Allows the initiator to grant the acceptor delegated credentials to act as the initiator's agent. Only the initiator can request delegation; the acceptor retrieves delegated credentials with getDelegCred(). Once delegation is requested, the mechanism provides delegation support if available.

Replay and Out-of-Sequence Detection: Requests message sequencing information so that per-message calls (getMIC, wrap) can detect replayed or reordered messages. Detected problems are reported via MessageProp methods like isDuplicateToken() and isUnseqToken().

Confidentiality (Encryption): For per-message operations, setPrivacy(true) in MessageProp requests encryption. The mechanism encrypts under the control of this flag.

Anonymity: Requests that the initiator's identity be hidden from the acceptor. Not all mechanisms support this. If unsupported, the initiator's identity is revealed despite the request.

Partial Context Protection: Some mechanisms allow per-message protection even before context establishment is complete. Calling isProtReady() indicates whether the context supports this.

Inter-Process Transfer: The export() method serializes a context to a byte array for transfer to another process. The isTransferable() method indicates if the context is transferable. After export, the original context becomes invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Before shaking hands, you can ask for: 'please identify yourself too' (mutual auth), 'I'll give you my powers' (delegation), 'watch for replayed messages' (replay detection), 'encrypt this' (confidentiality), 'hide my identity' (anonymity), or 'let me protect messages early' (pre-established protection).

sections.title: Error Reporting and Status Codes
sections.content:
Java GSS-API uses exceptions instead of status code returns. The GSSException class carries both major error codes (GSS-API level errors, independent of mechanism) and minor codes (mechanism-specific errors). Applications can retrieve error descriptions via getMajorString() and getMinorString().

Major error codes include: BAD_MECH (unsupported mechanism), BAD_NAME (invalid name), CONTEXT_EXPIRED (context lifetime exceeded), CREDENTIALS_EXPIRED (credentials have expired), DEFECTIVE_CREDENTIAL, DEFECTIVE_TOKEN, FAILURE (unspecified mechanism failure), NO_CONTEXT, NO_CRED, BAD_QOP (requested quality-of-protection unavailable), UNAUTHORIZED (operation forbidden by policy), UNAVAILABLE (operation or option unavailable), and token-related errors like DUPLICATE_TOKEN, OLD_TOKEN, UNSEQ_TOKEN, GAP_TOKEN (which are fatal during context establishment but informational during per-message calls).

For non-fatal per-message status, the MessageProp object returned from unwrap() and verifyMIC() contains supplementary status flags: isDuplicateToken(), isOldToken(), isUnseqToken(), isGapToken(). These inform the application but do not cause exceptions; the application must decide how to respond.
sections.plainLanguage: Errors are reported as exceptions with a major code (what failed) and a minor code (mechanism-specific details). For message protection, some issues like 'this is a old message' don't crash—they're reported in MessageProp so the app can decide what to do.

sections.title: Provider Framework and Mechanism Pluggability
sections.content:
GSS-API leverages the Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA) provider model, allowing implementations to be modular and extensible. Providers register themselves with the security framework and expose security services (like GSS-API mechanisms) for use by applications and other providers.

The GSSManager has methods to manage provider preferences: addProviderAtFront(provider, mech) prioritizes a provider for a specific mechanism or all mechanisms; addProviderAtEnd(provider, mech) uses a provider as a fallback. This lets applications ensure particular mechanisms are available without deep knowledge of the provider architecture.

Mechanisms can be added on a system-wide basis (available to all applications) or per-GSSManager instance (for custom implementations). The specification defers detailed Service Provider Interface (SPI) design to separate documents, allowing flexibility in implementation strategies.
sections.plainLanguage: Mechanisms are pluggable like printer drivers. Applications or the system can say 'when you need Kerberos, use Provider A first' or 'if nothing else works, try Provider B'. This lets new mechanisms be added without changing application code.
